## Atom-candidate and compiler contract

The candidate input contains one or more proposed atoms. Each candidate must include exactly the current
Atom Building Machinery fields:

```text
schema_version, atomic_step_id, outcome, practical_value,
stopping_condition, allowed_paths, captured_cases
```

The readiness wrapper additionally binds, outside the downstream request:

```text
requirement_ids, prerequisite_atom_ids, verification_ids,
authority_decision_ids, evidence_ids
```

Code rejects a candidate unless:

- it maps to at least one requirement and every requirement maps to at least one candidate acceptance
  boundary;
- its dependencies form a DAG and every prerequisite appears earlier in topological order;
- allowed paths are complete or an explicit path-discovery obligation blocks readiness;
- it has at least one immutable success case and one immutable rejection case unless a type-specific
  owner-approved exception exists;
- its verification route does not trust a producer verdict;
- no open linked blocker remains;
- its outcome, practical value, and stopping condition are non-empty and distinct duties are not hidden
  in one envelope; and
- the two blind atom-cohesion seats agree on `cohesive` using only registered IDs.

The compiler strips readiness-only wrapper fields and writes byte-stable downstream `atom-request.json`
files in dependency order. Each file matches the current Atom Controller `start REQUEST RUN` contract.
Candidate identity, ordering, request bytes, and aggregate sequence hash are recorded before readiness is
derived.

## Verdict, approval, and handoff

Per-requirement dispositions are:

```text
unresolved, satisfied, refuted, not-applicable, blocked, needs-owner
```

`not-applicable` requires an explicit provenance-bound owner or requirement-source record. Absence never
means not applicable.

The public verdict is derived, never written directly:

- `blocked`: any mandator

y non-owner condition, invalid model result, contradiction, missing planning or
  research result, graph cycle, verification gap, or open linked blocker remains;
- `needs_owner`: no `blocked` item remains and one owner-only decision is the queue head;
- `ready`: every requirement has a complete disposition, all evidence is fit, all contradictions and
  dependencies resolve, verification is complete and independent, candidate atoms are cohesive and
  ordered, package schema and replay pass, and no unresolved queue item remains.

Approval is a separate record:

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "atom_sequence_sha256": "...",
  "decision": "approved",
  "owner_record": {"path": "...", "sha256": "..."}
}
```

The controller accepts approval only while `ready` and only for the exact current sequence hash. Any
later change to inputs, graph, candidates, ordering, verification, or controller contract invalidates
approval by creating a new run identity.

`export-next-atom` succeeds only for `ready + approved`. It writes exactly one next atom request below
`WORK/handoff/<ordinal>-<atomic-step-id>/` plus a
handoff receipt containing the readiness package hash, sequence hash, atom ordinal, prior-atom
authorization requirement, and source request hash. It prints—but never runs—the exact Atom Controller
start command. Later atoms remain unavailable until the previous Atom Building Machinery authorization
receipt is admitted and verified.

For a successor atom, `admit-atom-completion` resolves the exact hash-bound Atom Controller source from
the run's admitted machinery contracts and invokes only:

```text
python3 <admitted-atom-controller.py> authorize-next <declared-atom-run>
```

The command is read-only. The readiness controller applies its execution timeout, captures stdout,
stderr, exit status, Atom Controller source hash, declared atom-run path, and current atom-run ledger hash,
and admits only the exact current response fields:

```text
schema_version, atomic_step_id, authorized, proof_event_sha256,
blocker_closeout_sha256, linked_blocker_occurrences
```

It requires `authorized: true`, the expected atom identity, a successful exit, and a proof event present
at the tip of the supplied run's append-only ledger. It snapshots the response and ledger bytes into the
readiness run. Immediately before exporting the successor it repeats the same read-only command; a
failure or changed proof/closeout identity invalidates the admission and blocks export. It never calls
`start`, `record-experiment`, `record-promotion`, `record-validation`, or any product command.

## Ledger and replay

`ledger.jsonl` is append-only, monotonically sequenced, and predecessor-hashed. Event schemas are closed.
The minimum event families are:

```text
run_started, input_admitted, adapter_completed,
node_registered, edge_registered, condition_classified,
evidence_requested, evidence_admitted, evidence_rejected,
interview_prepared, interview_admitted, interview_rejected,
owner_question_prepared, owner_answer_admitted, owner_answer_rejected,
owner_answer_superseded, queue_derived, verdict_derived,
atom_candidates_admitted, atom_candidates_rejected,
atom_sequence_compiled, package_prepared, package_compiled,
atom_sequence_approved, atom_sequence_rejected,
atom_completion_admitted, atom_completion_rejected, atom_handoff_exported
```

Events carry the prior and resulting state hashes where applicable. Timestamps are evidence but do not
participate in semantic queue ordering. Stored `graph.json`, `queue.json`, `verdict.json`, and package
files are rebuildable caches. `verify-replay` reconstructs them into a new scratch directory below the
run, byte-compares them with stored projections, records no event, and exits nonzero on any difference.

Every mutating failure after `run_started` writes one terminal command receipt with error kind and safe
evidence hashes. A command is never left looking active after its process exits.

## Readiness package

`compile-package` creates this immutable tree below the run:

```text
package/
  manifest.json
  ledger.jsonl
  graph.json
  requirements.json
  evidence.json
  decisions.json
  verification.json
  queue.json
  verdict.json
  atom-sequence.json
  atoms/<ordinal>-<atomic-step-id>/atom-request.json

`manifest.json` records every other relative path, byte count, SHA-256, schema version,
run/input/controller hash, readiness verdict, approval state, atom-sequence hash, and the exact live-
ledger prefix tip represented by `ledger.jsonl`. It does not list or hash itself. The SHA-256 of the
complete manifest bytes is the package-generation identity recorded in the live ledger and in any later
handoff. The package is write-once. Any update creates a new package generation whose predecessor
manifest hash is recorded.

Internally, a graph with no unresolved domain item enters `preparing-package`, while its public verdict
remains `blocked`. The controller appends `package_prepared`, closes that ledger prefix, renders the next
generation into a new staging directory, replays from the packaged prefix, verifies every closed schema
and member hash, then atomically renames staging to its immutable generation path. Only after that rename

that immutable package. A failed render leaves no final generation and appends a terminal failure receipt.

bind sequence for a new immutable generation containing that approval. Handoff names both the approved
generation's manifest hash and its `package_compiled` event. This avoids deriving readiness from a
package that does not yet exist or requiring a package to contain the event that hashes itself.

While blocked or awaiting the owner, `atom-sequence.json` and `atoms/` are absent; `queue.json` is
present. When ready, both are present and the queue is empty. `report.md` explains every requirement
verdict and displays exactly one actionable next item when not ready.

# Requirement-to-Atom Readiness Machinery — Decision-Complete Architecture

## Architecture verdict

Build one event-sourced controller around a typed dependency graph and one deterministic global queue.
The graph owns shared identity; requirement and phase views are read-only projections. Models answer only
one controller-generated semantic question per isolated process. The owner alone supplies authority and
approves the final atom-sequence hash. Atom Building Machinery receives nothing until both the replayed
readiness verdict is `ready` and that exact hash is `approved`.

This architecture adopts the RA-5 `graph-queue` result. It does not promote the research probe: the
production machinery is built from the contracts below and verified independently.

## System boundary

The machinery owns pre-implementation readiness only. It:

- admits and freezes declared inputs;
- imports the exact final Description and Requirements results through format-specific adapters;
- registers evidence, dependencies, authority decisions, contradictions, verification obligations, and
  candidate atoms in one graph;
- derives evidence fitness mechanically;
- prepares and admits bounded semantic interviews;
- exposes exactly one next external action while retaining the complete ordered unresolved queue;
- derives `blocked`, `needs_owner`, or `ready` by replay;
- compiles validated candidate atoms into the current Atom Building Machinery request schema;
- records owner approval against the exact atom-sequence hash; and
- exports approved atom requests one at a time for Atom Building Machinery.

It does not collect live AWS, database, or product evidence itself; perform open-ended research or
planning; mutate a target repository or external system; implement an atom; start or advance an Atom
Building Machinery run; commit; deploy; or infer owner authority. Its one permitted Atom Building call
is the existing read-only `authorize-next` stop-boundary check after an atom has completed.

Research and Plan remain direct work phases, never skills or controller dependencies. When either is
needed, the controller emits one provenance-bound request artifact and stops.

## Deployable source layout

```text
skills/requirement-to-atom-readiness-machinery/
  SKILL.md
  agents/openai.yaml
  references/
    request-contract.md
    graph-contract.md
    evidence-contract.md
    interview-contract.md
    atom-handoff-contract.md
  schemas/
    description-handoff.schema.json
    requirements-handoff.schema.json
    readiness-request.schema.json
    evidence-manifest.schema.json
    graph.schema.json
    owner-answer.schema.json
    model-response.schema.json
    atom-candidates.schema.json
    readiness-package.schema.json
  scripts/
    readiness_controller.py
    description_adapter.py
    requirements_adapter.py
    evidence_adapter.py
    model_interview.py
    package_renderer.py
tests/
  test_requirement_to_atom_readiness.py
```

Two additive upstream exporters are prerequisites, but are not part of this skill's write boundary:

```text
skills/description-machinery/scripts/export_handoff.py
skills/requirements-machinery/scripts/cover.py export-handoff ...
```

They add opt-in export commands only. Existing Description and Requirements commands, outputs, and
default flows remain unchanged.

`readiness_controller.py` is the only state writer. Adapters return validated values to the controller
and never append events. `model_interview.py` may write only inside one prepared attempt directory; it
cannot update the ledger. `package_renderer.py` reads replayed state and writes only through a
controller-issued output capability.

## Runtime root and write boundary

Every command requires an explicit absolute `--work` path. The controller rejects a work path that is:

- equal to, below, or above any declared target repository;
- equal to or below any declared product edit boundary;
- a symbolic link or contains a symbolic-link ancestor below the first existing parent;
- non-empty at `start`; or
- outside the owner-authorized runtime root recorded in the request.

All machinery writes remain below `--work`. The machinery never writes into a target repository,
`Tasks/`, a source evidence directory, or a temporary location not owned by the run. Final reports and
handoff files are part of the run and therefore durable. Copying them into a repository is a separate
owner-authorized action, not controller behavior.

Inputs are copied exactly once into a content-addressed run store. The controller does not recursively
copy a repository. Directories are inadmissible as evidence unless supplied as a deterministic manifest
whose members, sizes, and hashes are explicit. This prevents both product-surface contamination and
per-case bundle amplification seen in the retained Dropbox telemetry.

## Runtime and serialization contract

Version 1 is Python 3 standard-library code only. It adds no package-manager or runtime dependency.
JSON Schema files document every external contract, while the controller itself enforces exact keys,
types, enums, cardinalities, numeric bounds, and cross-record identities with code-owned validators.
The implementation must not depend on `jsonschema`; the retained missing-runtime failure proves that an
undeclared validator dependency would make the operator path non-replayable.

All state-bearing JSON is UTF-8 encoded, has no byte-order mark, and ends with one line feed. Canonical
JSON used for identity and hashing is serialized with sorted object keys and separators `(',', ':')`,
with no insignificant whitespace, before SHA-256. JSONL events use one independently canonical JSON
object plus one line feed per event. Human-readable projections may be indented, but their hashes cover
their actual bytes. IDs derived from content always name both the schema version and canonical input
fields in their contract so a later version cannot silently collide.

The running controller records `sys.executable`, its resolved regular-file identity, Python version, and
file hash at `start`; every subprocess uses that same interpreter. A resume under different interpreter
identity is refused rather than silently changing serialization or validation behavior.

The only v1 semantic provider is the installed OpenAI Codex CLI. At `start`, the controller resolves the
`codex` launcher from `PATH`, records the discovered launcher path and link target, requires the resolved
target to be a regular file, and records its real path, version output, and file hash. The request selects
an explicit model identifier and reasoning effort;
the launcher passes them to `codex exec` together with `--ignore-user-config`, `--ignore-rules`,
`--ephemeral`, `--skip-git-repo-check`, `--sandbox read-only`, `--output-schema`, and
`--output-last-message`; it supplies the model with `--model` and the effort with the strict configuration
override `-c model_reasoning_effort=<value>`. Provider abstraction, a second provider, or an implicit
host-de

fault model is a versioned extension, not an implementer option.

Each seat receives a newly created empty `WORK/model/<interview-id>/<seat>/cwd` and the launcher refuses
that directory if any repository or instruction-file ancestry is detected. Readiness-affecting semantic
families use exactly two blind seats. Owner-question wording uses exactly one seat. No other seat count is
valid in v1.

## Upstream handoff gap and additive exporters

Direct inspection established that current upstream outputs are not yet sufficient for a fail-closed
readiness declaration:

- Description writes `description.md`, `input-state.json`, `questions.json`, per-seat question records,
  and process feed entries, but no terminal machine-readable receipt binds the completed description
  bytes to the agreed reader set and input hashes.
- Requirements writes `requirements.md`, `coverage.json`, and a terminal feed event, but that event names
  the output path without binding its bytes. Its `document` command may update run state and deliberately
  refuses a copied run below `/private/tmp`, so the readiness controller cannot safely reconstruct the
  document inside its mandatory external runtime root.

The machinery therefore refuses an unsealed Description or Requirements input. It does not downgrade
the missing seal to a warning or implement an ad hoc Markdown-only trust path.

Both exporters require a caller-supplied absolute output path below the readiness run's authorized root
but outside the completed upstream run, every target repository, and every product edit boundary. They
open that output exclusively, refuse an existing file, and never edit, copy into, or append to the
completed upstream run. The readiness controller then admits the sealed file through the same hash-and-
snapshot path as every other input.

### Description handoff exporter

The additive exporter reads one completed Description run and writes one closed-schema handoff to an
explicit output path. It performs no model call and does not edit the completed run. It verifies all
eight question identities, both reader seats per question, exact quote agreement, source-byte matches,
input-state hashes, and final assembly. The handoff contains:

```text
schema_version, machinery, contract_version, run_identity,
input_state_sha256, questions_sha256, context_sha256,
reader_records[{question_id, seat, path, sha256, answer_sha256}],
description{path, sha256}, source_objects[{origin, sha256}],
terminal_state, exporter_source_sha256, handoff_sha256
```

`handoff_sha256` is the SHA-25

6 of the canonical object with the top-level `handoff_sha256` field
omitted. The caller separately supplies the SHA-256 of the complete handoff file in the readiness
request. The two values are different identities and both are verified.

The output path is audit identity only after admission; the readiness controller snapshots the handoff,
description, reader records, and sources into its run-owned store.

### Requirements handoff exporter

The additive `export-handoff` command reuses a refactored pure document-assembly function inside
Requirements Machinery. The existing `document` command calls the same function. The exporter reads a
completed run, reconstructs the final document in memory without a model call or state write, compares
the bytes to the named `requirements.md`, and writes:

```text
schema_version, machinery, contract_version, target,
source{path, sha256}, coverage_sha256, terminal_feed_entry_sha256,
requirements_document{path, sha256},

```

The Requirements handoff uses the same non-self-referential `handoff_sha256` rule. No schema may define
a digest over bytes that contain that digest.

`requirement_id` is `req-<first-16-of-sha256>` over canonical exact text plus sorted source anchors.
The exporter refuses any incomplete coverage, pending owner item, document mismatch, unparsed retained
or rejected item, or source drift.

These exporters solve provenance sealing only. They do not start readiness work, wire the new controller
into existing flows, or change whether upstream machinery runs.

## Graph contract

The canonical graph has six node types:

| Node | Owned fields |
| --- | --- |
| `requirement` | stable ID, ordinal, exact text, source anchors, maturity, disposition |
| `evidence` | stable ID, object hash, origin, capture and freshness data, claim, limitations, fitness |
| `authority_decision` | stable ID, authority owner, one question, answer contract, current admitted answer |
| `contradiction` | stable pair of claim IDs, source anchors, state, resolution authority |
| `verification` | stable ID, observable, success cases, rejection cases, execution route, independence rule |
| `atom_candidate` | stable ID, one outcome, boundaries, prerequisites, requirement and case mappings |

Allowed directed edge types are:

```text
supports, refutes, requires, governed-by, conflicts-with,
verified-by, maps-to-atom, precedes
```

Code creates every node and edge identity. A model may select only IDs already offered by a prepared
interview. Unknown nodes, duplicate edges, self-dependencies, wrong endpoint types, and cycles in
`requires` or `precedes` are refused.

The graph is stored as canonical JSON sorted by node ID and edge tuple. Every accepted mutation records
the before and after graph hashes in the ledger. Requirement pages and phase summaries are regenerated
views; editing them never changes state.

An evidence record contains:

```text

claim, limitations, affected_requirement_ids, required_maturity,
freshness_rule, access_receipt, reproduction_receipt,

Code derives these separate booleans: `present`, `hash_valid`, `accessible_at_capture`, `current`,

Database, AWS, Azure, Docker, or product probes are executed through an already-governed Sequence Runner

containing the exact claim, required fields, allowed source boundary, sequence identity when one exists,
and finite recovery condition. It does not reconstruct or run the operational command itself.

An external or temporary path is never fit evidence. The evidence manifest and every file it names are
copied into the run before registration. A producer verdict is audit data only and cannot satisfy a
verification node.

## Queue and scheduling contract

`advance` first exhausts safe deterministic transitions. It then sorts unresolved nodes by this fixed
tuple:

```text
(blocking class, dependency layer, earliest linked requirement ordinal,
 source ordinal, stable node id)
```

Blocking classes are ordered:

1. input, integrity, schema, or replay failure;
2. mandatory inaccessible, stale, missing, non-reproducible, or open-blocker evidence;
3. unresolved contradiction;
4. model-eligible semantic assessment;
5. direct research request;
6. direct planning request;
7. atom-candidate or verification completion;
8. owner-only authority decision.

The full ordered queue is retained in `queue.json`. The public `next_action` contains only its first
item. A report may state counts and dependencies but may not display multiple answerable questions at
once. Re-entering unchanged state returns the same next action and hash.

`blocked` outranks `needs_owner`: owner status is emitted only when no mandatory non-owner blocker is
ahead of it. This preserves the RA-3 rule that the owner is asked after currently machine-resolvable work
is settled.

Only these matters are owner-only: legal basis, consent and retention, business rules, scope expansion,

## Atom-candidate and compiler contract

The candidate input contains one or more proposed atoms. Each candidate must include exactly the current
Atom Building Machinery fields:

```text
schema_version, atomic_step_id, outcome, practical_value,
stopping_condition, allowed_paths, captured_cases
```

The readiness wrapper additionally binds, outside the downstream request:

```text
requirement_ids, prerequisite_atom_ids, verification_ids,
authority_decision_ids, evidence_ids
```

Code rejects a candidate unless:

- it maps to at least one requirement and every requirement maps to at least one candidate acceptance
  boundary;
- its dependencies form a DAG and every prerequisite appears earlier in topological order;
- allowed paths are complete or an explicit path-discovery obligation blocks readiness;
- it has at least one immutable success case and one immutable rejection case unless a type-specific
  owner-approved exception exists;
- its verification route does not trust a producer verdict;
- no open linked blocker remains;
- its outcome, practical value, and stopping condition are non-empty and distinct duties are not hidden
  in one envelope; and
- the two blind atom-cohesion seats agree on `cohesive` using only registered IDs.

The compiler strips readiness-only wrapper fields and writes byte-stable downstream `atom-request.json`
files in dependency order. Each file matches the current Atom Controller `start REQUEST RUN` contract.
Candidate identity, ordering, request bytes, and aggregate sequence hash are recorded before readiness is
derived.

Per-requirement dispositions are:

```text
unresolved, satisfied, refuted, not-applicable, blocked, needs-owner
```

`not-applicable` requires an explicit provenance-bound owner or requirement-source record. Absence never
means not applicable.

The public verdict is derived, never written directly:

- `blocked`: any mandator

y non-owner condition, invalid model result, contradiction, missing planning or
  research result, graph cycle, verification gap, or open linked blocker remains;
- `needs_owner`: no `blocked` item remains and one owner-only decision is the queue head;
- `ready`: every requirement has a complete disposition, all evidence is fit, all contradictions and
  dependencies resolve, verification is complete and independent, candidate atoms are cohesive and
  ordered, package schema and replay pass, and no unresolved queue item remains.

Approval is a separate record:

```json

  "atom_sequence_sha256": "...",
  "decision": "approved",

}

later change to inputs, graph, candidates, ordering, verification, or controller contract invalidates
approval by creating a new run identity.

handoff receipt containing the readiness package hash, sequence hash, atom ordinal, prior-atom

`ledger.jsonl` is append-only, monotonically sequenced, and predecessor-hashed. Event schemas are closed.

interview_prepared, interview_admitted, interview_rejected,

Every mutating failure after `run_started` writes one terminal command receipt with error kind and safe

## Readiness package

`compile-package` creates this immutable tree below the run:

```text
package/
  manifest.json
  ledger.jsonl
  graph.json
  requirements.json
  evidence.json
  decisions.json
  verification.json
  queue.json
  verdict.json
  atom-sequence.json
  atoms/<ordinal>-<atomic-step-id>/atom-request.json
  report.md
  replay-receipt.json
```

`manifest.json` records every other relative path, byte count, SHA-256, schema version,
run/input/controller hash, readiness verdict, approval state, atom-sequence hash, and the exact live-
ledger prefix tip represented by `ledger.jsonl`. It does not list or hash itself. The SHA-256 of the
complete manifest bytes is the package-generation identity recorded in the live ledger and in any later
handoff. The package is write-once. Any update creates a new package generation whose predecessor
manifest hash is recorded.

Internally, a graph with no unresolved domain item enters `preparing-package`, while its public verdict
remains `blocked`. The controller appends `package_prepared`, closes that ledger prefix, renders the next
generation into a new staging directory, replays from the packaged prefix, verifies every closed schema
and member hash, then atomically renames staging to its immutable generation path. Only after that rename
does it append `package_compiled` with the complete manifest hash and derive `ready`. Thus the packaged
ledger intentionally ends at `package_prepared`; the live ledger suffix is the external receipt binding
that immutable package. A failed render leaves no final generation and appends a terminal failure receipt.

`approve-atoms` first appends the owner approval, then repeats the same prepare/render/verify/finalize/
bind sequence for a new immutable generation containing that approval. Handoff names both the approved
generation's manifest hash and its `package_compiled` event. This avoids deriving readiness from a
package that does not yet exist or requiring a package to contain the event that hashes itself.

While blocked or awaiting the owner, `atom-sequence.json` and `atoms/` are absent; `queue.json` is
present. When ready, both are present and the queue is empty. `report.md` explains every requirement
verdict and displays exactly one actionable next item when not ready.
